title: Philippians in 7 Days
subtitle: Joy that doesn't depend on circumstances
tagline: A letter of joy, written in chains.
about: Paul wrote Philippians from custody to a church that had stood with him from the start. In one week you will read the whole letter: its thanks, its portrait of Christ's humility, its warnings, and its secret of contentment. You will come away seeing how joy, partnership, and the mind of Christ fit together.

days.title: Partners in the Gospel
days.focus: Notice how much gratitude and joy fill Paul's opening, even though he is writing from custody. Watch the word 'fellowship' and listen to what Paul prays for: love that grows in knowledge and discernment.
days.context: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, and the church began during Paul's visit described in Acts 16. Paul writes while imprisoned, traditionally in Rome around AD 60–62, though some scholars suggest Ephesus or Caesarea.

word.why: Paul thanks God for their 'fellowship in the gospel from the first day' (v. 5). The word describes a shared stake in something; the Philippians had partnered with Paul through prayer and gifts, not just friendship.

questions.q: What is Paul confident God will do in the Philippians (v. 6)?
Why might Paul pray for love that abounds 'in knowledge and in all judgment' rather than simply for more love?
Who has been a partner with you in faith, and what has that partnership looked like?

checkIn.q: Which city's church is this letter written to?
Who is named alongside Paul in the first verse?

days.title: To Live Is Christ
days.focus: Paul turns news of his imprisonment into a report of gospel progress. Watch how he weighs living against dying, and how he calls the church to live in a way 'as it becometh the gospel of Christ.'
days.context: The 'palace' in verse 13 refers to the praetorium, the imperial guard or governor's headquarters. Soldiers guarding Paul in shifts would have heard why he was there.

word.why: Paul uses this word at both ends of the passage: his chains have led to the 'furtherance of the gospel' (v. 12), and he expects to remain for the Philippians' 'furtherance and joy of faith' (v. 25). Progress, not setback, is how he reads his situation.

questions.q: What two results of his imprisonment does Paul describe in verses 13–14?
What does Paul mean when he says 'to live is Christ, and to die is gain' (v. 21)?
If your current circumstances were measured by whether Christ is honored in them rather than by whether they are comfortable, how would they look?

checkIn.q: According to Paul, what has his imprisonment led to?
What does Paul say would be 'far better'?
options: To depart and be with Christ

days.title: The Mind of Christ
days.focus: Paul moves from a call to unity and humility into a poetic description of Christ. Trace the downward steps (form of God, servant, death, cross), then notice the turn upward: 'Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.'
days.context: Many scholars think verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn or poem that Paul either quotes or composed himself. Its rhythm stands out even in English.

word.meaning: to empty, to make of no reputation
word.why: The KJV says Christ 'made himself of no reputation' (v. 7); the Greek literally says he 'emptied himself.' Christians have long discussed what this involved, but the passage explains it in its own terms: he took the form of a servant and humbled himself to death.

questions.q: List the steps Christ takes downward in verses 6–8.
How does the story of Christ in verses 6–11 answer the call to humility in verses 3–4?
Where do you find it hardest to look 'on the things of others' and not only your own?

checkIn.q: What kind of death does Paul say Christ accepted?
options: A peaceful death in old age

checkIn.q: According to verses 10–11, what will every tongue confess?

days.title: Shining as Lights
days.focus: Paul calls the church to 'work out' their salvation, while insisting that God is the one at work in them. Then he introduces two coworkers, Timothy and Epaphroditus, as living examples of the selflessness he has just described.
days.context: Epaphroditus had carried the Philippians' gift to Paul and fell so ill that he nearly died. Paul sends him home, partly because the church had heard of his illness and was worried.

word.meaning: to work out, to carry through to completion
word.why: Paul says 'work out your own salvation' and immediately adds 'for it is God which worketh in you' (vv. 12–13). The verb is about bringing something to its finish, not earning it; the passage holds human effort and God's work together.

questions.q: What reason does Paul give in verse 13 for working out salvation 'with fear and trembling'?
Why do you think Paul follows his teaching on humility with the stories of Timothy and Epaphroditus?
Is there an area of your life where murmuring or disputing (v. 14) has become a habit?

checkIn.q: Who was sick, 'nigh unto death,' while serving Paul?
Paul says the Philippians shine in the world as what?

days.title: Counting Loss as Gain
days.focus: Paul warns against teachers who insisted Gentile believers be circumcised, then lists his own impressive credentials, only to count them as loss. Notice what he wants instead: to know Christ and be found in him.
days.context: Some teachers claimed Gentile Christians needed circumcision and law-keeping to belong fully to God's people. Paul's sharp language in verse 2 ('dogs,' 'the concision') is aimed at that teaching.

word.why: Paul says he counts his former advantages as 'dung' (v. 8), a deliberately blunt word for what gets thrown out. The shock is the point: next to knowing Christ, even his best credentials are worthless as a basis for standing before God.

questions.q: Name three items from Paul's list of credentials in verses 5–6.
What is the difference between a righteousness 'of mine own' and the righteousness 'which is of God by faith' (v. 9)?
What achievements or identities are you most tempted to lean on for your standing before God?

checkIn.q: Which tribe does Paul say he comes from?
According to verse 10, what does Paul want to know?
options: Christ and the power of his resurrection

days.title: Citizens of Heaven
days.focus: Paul admits he has not arrived, and pictures himself as a runner straining toward the finish. Notice the contrast between those 'whose God is their belly' and those whose citizenship is in heaven.
days.context: Philippi's residents prized their Roman citizenship, which the colony enjoyed even though Rome was far away. Paul's readers would have heard 'our citizenship is in heaven' against that background.

word.why: The KJV renders it 'conversation' (v. 20), an older English word for one's way of life, but the Greek refers to belonging to a state. In a proud Roman colony, Paul tells believers their true homeland is heaven, from which they await a Savior.

questions.q: What does Paul say he does with 'those things which are behind' (v. 13)?
How does a heavenly citizenship shape the way Paul speaks about the body in verse 21?
What from your past most often pulls your attention backward?

checkIn.q: According to verse 21, what will Christ do to 'our vile body'?
options: Change it to be like his glorious body

checkIn.q: What does Paul say he presses toward?
options: A place of honor in Rome
The prize of the high calling of God

days.title: Rejoice, Pray, Be Content
days.focus: Paul urges two women to agree, calls the church to rejoice and to pray instead of being anxious, then thanks them for their gift. Notice that his 'secret' of contentment is something he learned, and that it rests on Christ's strength.
days.context: Euodias and Syntyche had labored alongside Paul in the gospel; their disagreement was serious enough that Paul names them and asks a coworker to help. 'Caesar's household' (v. 22) likely means slaves and officials in imperial service, not the emperor's family.

word.why: Greek philosophers used this word for a person who needed nothing outside himself. Paul borrows it but changes its source: 'I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me' (v. 13).

questions.q: What does Paul tell the church to do instead of being anxious (v. 6)?
How does verse 13 sound different when read alongside verses 11–12 rather than on its own?
Which of the things listed in verse 8 gets the least of your attention?

checkIn.q: Which two women does Paul ask to be of the same mind?
What does Paul say he has learned?
options: To be content in whatever state he is in

leader.intro: Philippians is short enough to read in one sitting, so encourage your group to read the whole letter at least once during the week alongside the daily passages. Plan about 60–75 minutes: 10 minutes to settle in, 40–50 minutes of discussion, and 10–15 minutes to pray. Consider reading Philippians 2:5-11 aloud together to open; it is the heart of the letter. You will not get through every question, and that is fine; aim to let the letter's joy and its picture of Christ's humility sink in.

sessions.title: Joy, Humility, and Contentment
sessions.opening: What is something small that reliably brings you joy, even on a hard day?
discussion: Paul is in custody, yet the words 'joy' and 'rejoice' run through the whole letter. Where did you notice them this week?
In chapter 1, how does Paul interpret his imprisonment? What does he count as success?
Read 2:5-11 aloud. What does this passage tell us about who Jesus is, and about what humility looks like?
Paul says 'work out your own salvation' and 'it is God which worketh in you' in the same breath (2:12-13). How do these fit together?
In chapter 3 Paul lists everything he once relied on. What would a modern version of that list look like?
What do you think Paul means by 'I have learned... to be content' (4:11)? How is that different from simply not caring?
Which verse from this letter do you most want to carry into next week, and why?
sessions.notes: The church in Philippi began in Acts 16 with Lydia, a slave girl set free, and a jailer and his household; it was a mixed group from the start, and it supported Paul financially more than once (4:15-16). The letter is partly a thank-you note for their latest gift, carried by Epaphroditus. Two common confusions are worth heading off. First, 2:12 ('work out your own salvation') does not mean earning salvation; the next verse grounds it in God's work, and the word describes carrying something through to completion. Second, 4:13 is often quoted as a promise of success in any goal, but in context it is about contentment in both plenty and need. Groups can get stuck debating exactly what Christ 'emptied himself' of in 2:7; thoughtful Christians have explained it in different ways, so gently steer back to what the text itself says: he took the form of a servant and went to the cross. If someone is struggling with anxiety, 4:6-7 can feel like pressure; it may help to note that Paul pairs it with prayer and thanksgiving, not willpower.
sessions.prayer: Bring specific worries to God together with thanksgiving (4:6), and give thanks for the people who have been partners with you in the gospel.
